FORM OF WAGE PAYMENT: CHECKS, SCRIP, DIRECT DEPOSIT, AND PAYROLL CARDS (LAB. CODE §§ 212–213) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
Acme, Inc. maintains this information sheet to describe what California law says about the form in which wages may be paid to an employee such as Jordan Lee — that is, not when or how much must be paid, but what kind of instrument or method an employer may use to deliver the pay. It describes the governing statute (Labor Code section 212), which restricts payment by check or other instrument to instruments that are negotiable and payable in cash, on demand, without discount, at an established place of business in California, and which prohibits payment in scrip, coupons, or cards redeemable in merchandise; the statutory exceptions in Labor Code section 213, including voluntarily authorized direct deposit; the criminal and civil-penalty provisions attached to section 212; the published court decisions and Labor Commissioner opinion letter addressing out-of-state paychecks and payroll debit cards; and the related federal rule that an account at a particular institution may not be required as a condition of employment. It describes the law; it does not select, authorize, or change any method of payment.

LABOR CODE SECTION 212: WAGE INSTRUMENTS MUST BE NEGOTIABLE, PAYABLE IN CASH ON DEMAND, WITHOUT DISCOUNT
Labor Code section 212(a)(1) provides that no person, or agent or officer of a person, may issue in payment of wages due, or to become due, or as an advance on wages to be earned, any order, check, draft, note, memorandum, or other acknowledgment of indebtedness unless it meets each of several conditions: it is negotiable; it is payable in cash, on demand, without discount, at some established place of business in the state; the name and address of that place of business appear on the instrument; and, at the time of issuance and for a reasonable time afterward that must be at least 30 days, the maker or drawer has sufficient funds in, or a credit, arrangement, or understanding with, the drawee for its payment. A neighboring provision, Labor Code section 208, states that all payments of wages are to be made in the manner provided by law. The Court of Appeal has described section 212 as a measure essentially intended to prevent employers from giving employees paychecks that cannot be cashed, and has summarized its accepted purpose as preventing payment of wages by orders payable only in goods or of an indefinite nature not payable on demand, or by paychecks that cannot be honored because of the drawee's insufficient funds.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-11]
  "No person, or agent or officer thereof, shall issue in payment of wages due, or to become due, or as an advance on wages to be earned: (1) Any order, check, draft, note, memorandum, or other acknowledgment of indebtedness, unless it is negotiable and payable in cash, on demand, without discount, at some established place of business in the state, the name and address of which must appear on the instrument, and at the time of its issuance and for a reasonable time thereafter, which must be at least 30 days, the maker or drawer has sufficient funds in, or credit, arrangement, or understanding with the drawee for its payment."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 212(a) (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Lab. Code § 212(a)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=212.)
  "All payments shall be made in the manner provided by law."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 208 (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Lab. Code § 208 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=208.)
  "We also reject CCPOA’s contention that the furlough program contravenes Labor Code section 212, a measure essentially intended to prevent employers from giving employees paychecks that cannot be cashed."
  — Brown v. Superior Court (Cal. Ct. App. 2011), 199 Cal.App.4th 971 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5810606/brown-v-superior-court/)
  "The accepted purpose of Labor Code section 212 is to prevent employers from paying wages “by giving orders . . . payable only in goods, or orders of an indefinite nature not payable on demand, but at some future time” (In re Ballestra (1916) 173 Cal. 657, 658 [ 161 P. 120 ]), or paychecks which cannot be honored because of the drawee’s insufficient funds."
  — Brown v. Superior Court (Cal. Ct. App. 2011), 199 Cal.App.4th 971 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5810606/brown-v-superior-court/)
  "Those three cited cases represent the sum total of reported California decisions discussing this statute in the 75 years of its existence. And all have done so within the context of criminal prosecutions, because Labor Code section 215 makes it a misdemeanor to violate Labor Code section 212."
  — Brown v. Superior Court (Cal. Ct. App. 2011), 199 Cal.App.4th 971 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5810606/brown-v-superior-court/)
  Known gap: Section 212(a)(1) is quoted in full. The statute uses the terms "negotiable," "instrument," and "discount" without defining them; the DLSE opinion letter described in a later clause notes that the Labor Code does not define "instrument" or "negotiable" and looks to ordinary and legal-dictionary meanings. The Brown decision quoted here arose from a public-employee furlough dispute in which the court ultimately held section 212 had no application to accrued furlough credits; its description of the statute's purpose is quoted for that description only. Brown also observed that, as of 2011, only three reported California decisions (In re Ballestra (1916), People v. Turner (1957), and People v. Hampton (1965)) had discussed the statute in its 75-year existence, all in criminal prosecutions; the federal district court decision in Solis v. Regis Corp., described in a later clause, is not a California appellate decision and is not binding on California courts.

THE BAN ON SCRIP, COUPONS, AND CARDS REDEEMABLE IN MERCHANDISE
Labor Code section 212(a)(2) separately prohibits issuing, in payment of wages, any scrip, coupon, cards, or other thing redeemable in merchandise or purporting to be payable or redeemable otherwise than in money. This is the provision historically aimed at "company store" practices. In People v. Hampton (1965), the Court of Appeal quoted the California Supreme Court's 1916 explanation of the predecessor statute: the Legislature could be presumed to have acted because some employers had adopted the custom of paying wages by giving orders payable only in goods, or orders of an indefinite nature not payable on demand but at some future time, and the purpose of the statute was evidently to prevent the evils believed to have arisen from those practices. Hampton also adopted the Turner court's observation that the statute does not punish a failure to pay wages as such, but rather the act of undertaking to pay them by issuing an instrument that does not conform to the statute.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-11]
  "(2) Any scrip, coupon, cards, or other thing redeemable, in merchandise or purporting to be payable or redeemable otherwise than in money."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 212(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Lab. Code § 212(a)(2) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=212.)
  "In considering this statute we may presume, in support of the legislative enactment, that some employers in this state had adopted and followed the custom of paying the daily, weekly, or monthly wages of their employees, when due, by giving orders for the amount thereof payable only in goods, or orders of an indefinite nature not payable on demand, but at some future time. The purpose of the statute evidently is to prevent the evils which the legislature believed had arisen from such practices."
  — People v. Hampton (Cal. Ct. App. 1965), 236 Cal.App.2d 795 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2214097/people-v-hampton/)
  "It is to be noted that it does not purport to inflict punishment for failure to pay wages, but for undertaking to pay them by the issuance of some instrument."
  — People v. Hampton (Cal. Ct. App. 1965), 236 Cal.App.2d 795 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2214097/people-v-hampton/)
  "But we are not considering scrip for the company store, rubber checks, or criminal liability."
  — Brown v. Superior Court (Cal. Ct. App. 2011), 199 Cal.App.4th 971 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5810606/brown-v-superior-court/)
  Known gap: The historical rationale quoted in Hampton is the Court of Appeal's quotation of In re Ballestra (1916) 173 Cal. 657, and the "does not purport to inflict punishment for failure to pay wages" passage is Hampton's quotation, with its own bracketed modifications elsewhere in the passage, of People v. Turner (1957) 154 Cal.App.2d Supp. 883; neither Ballestra nor Turner was fetched directly for this document, so both are cited only as quoted within Hampton. The phrase "company store" is descriptive language drawn from Brown v. Superior Court's characterization ("scrip for the company store") and is not a statutory term. Whether a modern payroll debit card is a "card ... redeemable ... otherwise than in money" within section 212(a)(2) is addressed by the DLSE opinion letter described in a later clause, not by any published appellate decision located for this document.

THE IN-STATE PLACE OF BUSINESS REQUIREMENT AND OUT-OF-STATE PAYCHECKS
Section 212(a)(1) requires that a wage instrument be payable in cash, on demand, without discount, at some established place of business in the state, and that the name and address of that place of business appear on the instrument. Section 212(c) modifies the address element when the drawee is a bank: the bank's address need not appear on the instrument, and in that case the instrument must be negotiable and payable in cash, on demand, without discount, at any place of business of the drawee chosen by the person entitled to enforce it. In Solis v. Regis Corp. (N.D. Cal. 2007), a federal district court applied these provisions to a California employer whose payroll checks were drawn on a Chicago bank. The court noted it was undisputed that under federal law banks may hold out-of-state checks for up to five days, and held that the employer violated section 212 by paying employees with checks that did not provide the name and address of a California business that would cash the checks on demand and without discount — regardless of whether a given employee was actually injured. The court also held that a fee the named plaintiff paid to cash her checks had to be construed as a "discount" within the meaning of the statute.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-11]
  "Notwithstanding paragraph (1) of subdivision (a), if the drawee is a bank, the bank’s address need not appear on the instrument and, in that case, the instrument shall be negotiable and payable in cash, on demand, without discount, at any place of business of the drawee chosen by the person entitled to enforce the instrument."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 212(c) (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Lab. Code § 212(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=212.)
  "Plaintiff moves for summary judgment of liability on her claim that defendants violated California Labor Code section 212 by paying its subsidiaries’ employees with out-of-state checks. After carefully considering the parties’ papers, and having had the benefit of oral argument, the Court finds that defendants violated section 212."
  — Solis v. Regis Corp. (N.D. Cal. 2007), 612 F.Supp.2d 1085 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2494112/solis-v-regis-corp/)
  "It is undisputed that under federal law banks may hold out-of-state checks for up to five days."
  — Solis v. Regis Corp. (N.D. Cal. 2007), 612 F.Supp.2d 1085 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2494112/solis-v-regis-corp/)
  "Regardless of whether a class member was injured, defendants violated the statute by paying employees with checks that did not provide the name and address of a California business that would cash the checks on demand and without discount."
  — Solis v. Regis Corp. (N.D. Cal. 2007), 612 F.Supp.2d 1085 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2494112/solis-v-regis-corp/)
  "In addition, plaintiff is entitled to summary judgment on her own claim that she paid a fee at times to cash her checks; such fee must be construed as a “discount.”"
  — Solis v. Regis Corp. (N.D. Cal. 2007), 612 F.Supp.2d 1085 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2494112/solis-v-regis-corp/)
  Known gap: Solis is a decision of a federal district court on a motion for summary judgment as to liability, not a California appellate decision, and it is not binding on California courts; no published California appellate decision applying section 212 to out-of-state checks was located for this document. The court's reference to a five-day hold under federal law is stated in the opinion as undisputed between the parties; the underlying federal funds-availability rule was not fetched or verified for this document. Section 212(c), which the Solis opinion quotes only in part, was added by a 1997 amendment; the opinion's quotation of section 212(a)(1) uses ellipses and contains an apparent transposition ("unless is it negotiable") that is not reproduced here.

THE 30-DAY SUFFICIENT-FUNDS REQUIREMENT AND THE PRESUMPTION FROM A DISHONORED CHECK
Section 212(a)(1) requires that, at the time a wage instrument is issued and for a reasonable time afterward — which must be at least 30 days — the maker or drawer have sufficient funds in, or a credit, arrangement, or understanding with, the drawee for its payment. Section 212(b) supplies an evidentiary rule for enforcement: where an instrument is protested or dishonored, the notice or memorandum of protest or dishonor is admissible as proof of presentation, nonpayment, and protest, and is presumptive evidence of knowledge of insufficiency of funds or credit with the drawee. In People v. Hampton (1965), a criminal prosecution of employers whose payroll checks were dishonored, the Court of Appeal held that section 212(a) does not impose absolute criminal liability without regard to fault, but that once the prosecution establishes the facts giving rise to the statutory presumption, the burden shifts to the defendant to present evidence of justification. The court stated that an employer who pays by check is chargeable with knowledge of all that the employer reasonably should have known as well as what the employer actually knew, and must show that nonpayment of the checks resulted from circumstances neither foreseeable nor preventable by reasonably prudent investigation or action.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-11]
  "Where an instrument mentioned in subdivision (a) is protested or dishonored, the notice or memorandum of protest or dishonor is admissible as proof of presentation, nonpayment and protest and is presumptive evidence of knowledge of insufficiency of funds or credit with the drawee."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 212(b) (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Lab. Code § 212(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=212.)
  "We conclude, therefore, that while section 212, subdivision (a) does not impose an absolute criminal liability which completely precludes all possible defenses after it has been established that the proscribed act has been committed, it does validly establish the quantum of proof sufficient to sustain a conviction unless and until it is overcome by proof that the conduct of the defendant was neither wilfully wrong nor culpably negligent."
  — People v. Hampton (Cal. Ct. App. 1965), 236 Cal.App.2d 795 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2214097/people-v-hampton/)
  "He will be chargeable under section 212, subdivision (a) with knowledge of all that he reasonably should have known as well as that which he actually knew. To raise the issue of justification or excuse in a prosecution under this section, he must make some showing that the nonpayment of the checks was the result of circumstances neither foreseeable nor preventable by reasonably prudent investigation or action."
  — People v. Hampton (Cal. Ct. App. 1965), 236 Cal.App.2d 795 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2214097/people-v-hampton/)
  Known gap: Hampton is a 1965 decision construing the criminal application of section 212(a) as the statute then read; the statute has since been renumbered internally (the dishonor provision quoted in Hampton as the section's concluding sentence is now subdivision (b)) and amended in 1997 to add subdivision (c), but the sufficient-funds and dishonor language quoted here is materially the same. Hampton also distinguished section 212 from Penal Code section 476a (issuing checks without sufficient funds), noting that section 212 does not require proof of intent to defraud; that discussion is not quoted here. Labor Code section 203.1, which Hampton mentions and which imposes penalty wages on building and construction industry employers whose payroll checks are dishonored, was not fetched for this document and is not addressed.

ENFORCEMENT: MISDEMEANOR LIABILITY AND THE SECTION 225.5 CIVIL PENALTY
Two enforcement provisions attach to section 212. Labor Code section 215 makes any person, or the agent, manager, superintendent, or officer of a person, who violates section 212 (among other listed sections) guilty of a misdemeanor. Labor Code section 225.5 provides that, in addition to and independent of any other penalty in the article, every person who unlawfully withholds wages due any employee in violation of section 212, 216, 221, 222, or 223 is subject to a civil penalty of $100 for each failure to pay each employee for an initial violation, and $200 for each failure to pay each employee plus 25 percent of the amount unlawfully withheld for each subsequent, willful, or intentional violation; the penalty is recovered by the Labor Commissioner in a wage hearing or an independent civil action brought in the name of the people of the State of California. In Solis v. Regis Corp., the federal district court read the section 225.5 penalty as limited to section 212 violations that actually involve a withholding of wages — such as a check-cashing fee or a bank hold — and held that where an employee cashed the check on demand without a fee there was no withholding even if the check was drawn on an out-of-state bank; for section 212 violations not involving a withholding, the court concluded the default civil penalty of the Private Attorneys General Act (Labor Code section 2699(f)) applied instead.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-11]
  "Any person, or the agent, manager, superintendent or officer thereof, who violates any provision of Section 201.3, 204, 204b, 205, 207, 208, 209, or 212 is guilty of a misdemeanor."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 215 (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Lab. Code § 215 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=215.)
  "In addition to, and entirely independent and apart from, any other penalty provided in this article, every person who unlawfully withholds wages due any employee in violation of Section 212, 216, 221, 222, or 223 shall be subject to a civil penalty as follows: (a) For any initial violation, one hundred dollars ($100) for each failure to pay each employee. (b) For each subsequent violation, or any willful or intentional violation, two hundred dollars ($200) for each failure to pay each employee, plus 25 percent of the amount unlawfully withheld. The penalty shall be recovered by the Labor Commissioner as part of a hearing held to recover unpaid wages and penalties or in an independent civil action."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 225.5 (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Lab. Code § 225.5 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=225.5.)
  "In sum, in this matter of apparent first impression, the mandatory penalties of section 225.5 are limited to violations of section 212 that involve the withholding of wages. If an employee cashed her check on demand and without fee there was no withholding of wages, even if the check was made on an out-of-state bank."
  — Solis v. Regis Corp. (N.D. Cal. 2007), 612 F.Supp.2d 1085 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2494112/solis-v-regis-corp/)
  "Section 225.5, however, provides a specific penalty for only those violations which involve the withholding of wages due any employee; as the Court explained above, and as urged by defendants, it does not provide a specific penalty for violations of section 212 that do not involve the withholding of wages. Thus, section 2699(f) applies."
  — Solis v. Regis Corp. (N.D. Cal. 2007), 612 F.Supp.2d 1085 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2494112/solis-v-regis-corp/)
  Known gap: Section 225.5 is quoted in its penalty portions; its allocation of recovered penalties (12.5 percent to a Labor and Workforce Development Agency employer-education fund, the remainder to the General Fund) is in the statute but not quoted. Solis's reading of section 225.5 and its application of Labor Code section 2699(f) are the views of a federal district court in what the court itself called a matter of apparent first impression, and are not binding on California courts; the PAGA provisions the court applied have been amended several times since 2007, most recently in 2024, and the current text of section 2699 was not fetched for this document. Section 216, also listed in section 225.5, separately makes it a misdemeanor to willfully refuse to pay wages due after demand, or to falsely deny their amount or validity; it was fetched but is not quoted here.

LABOR CODE SECTION 213(D): VOLUNTARILY AUTHORIZED DIRECT DEPOSIT
Labor Code section 213 lists what section 212 does not do. Under subdivision (d), nothing in section 212 prohibits an employer from depositing wages due or to become due, or an advance on wages to be earned, in an account in any bank, savings and loan association, or credit union of the employee's choice with a place of business located in this state, provided that the employee has voluntarily authorized that deposit. The same subdivision adds that when an employee is discharged or quits, the employer may pay the wages then earned and unpaid by a deposit authorized under the subdivision, provided the employer complies with the article's provisions on payment of wages upon termination or quitting. The Labor Commissioner's office, in a 2008 opinion letter, read section 213(d) as the Legislature's specific authorization of direct deposit as a payment method with its own conditions, independent of the negotiable-instrument conditions in section 212(a), and described employee choice as a fundamental condition for payment methods using direct deposit under California wage payment law.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-11]
  "Prohibit an employer from depositing wages due or to become due or an advance on wages to be earned in an account in any bank, savings and loan association, or credit union of the employee’s choice with a place of business located in this state, provided that the employee has voluntarily authorized that deposit."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 213(d) (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Lab. Code § 213(d) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=213.)
  "It is clear from the language in Labor Code § 213(d) that the Legislature specifically authorized wage payments using direct deposit and prescribed the conditions for such payment method, and further, that Labor Code § 212 cannot be read to prohibit such wage payment method."
  — DLSE Opinion Letter 2008.07.07, Payroll/Debit Cards — Payment of Wages, Labor Code §§ 212 and 213 (July 7, 2008), DLSE Op. Letter 2008.07.07, at 5–6 (https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/opinions/2008-07-07.pdf)
  "Employee choice is thus a fundamental condition for payment methods utilizing direct deposits under California wage payment law."
  — DLSE Opinion Letter 2008.07.07, Payroll/Debit Cards — Payment of Wages, Labor Code §§ 212 and 213 (July 7, 2008), DLSE Op. Letter 2008.07.07, at 6 (https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/opinions/2008-07-07.pdf)
  Known gap: Section 213(d) is quoted in full. The statute's two conditions — an account at an institution of the employee's choice with a place of business in California, and the employee's voluntary authorization — are stated without further definition; the DLSE letter's reading of "place of business" is described in the payroll-card clause below. The final-pay sentence of section 213(d) is addressed in this project's separate Final Paycheck Delivery Method information sheet and is summarized rather than quoted here. This project's separate Direct Deposit Authorization document is a drafting form and cites no authority; this clause supplies the statutory basis it rests on. The DLSE opinion letter is an agency interpretation, not a statute or court decision, and its weight is discussed in the payroll-card clause's gap note.

PAYROLL DEBIT CARDS: THE LABOR COMMISSIONER'S 2008 OPINION LETTER AND THE MARENCO LITIGATION
No California statute specifically addresses payroll debit cards, and no published California appellate decision located for this document decides whether a particular payroll-card program complies with sections 212 and 213. The most detailed public authority is a July 7, 2008 opinion letter of the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement analyzing two national payroll-card programs. The letter treated the programs first as direct deposit under section 213(d) — concluding that the voluntariness condition was satisfied because employee participation was optional and employees retained the option of direct deposit to an institution of their own choosing — and then applied the section 212(a) requirement that wages be payable in cash without discount to the card itself. The letter stated that imposing a fee to access one's earned wages under such a program could impermissibly interfere with receipt of paid wages by reducing or discounting them, but concluded that programs providing at least one fee-free transaction per pay period, giving the employee access to full wages in cash on the scheduled payday, did not violate the wage payment provisions as described, and that their effectiveness in practice would require that employees be fully informed and that the card be presented as an optional alternative. The letter also stated that the itemized wage statement requirement of Labor Code section 226(a) continues to apply. The fact pattern the letter warned about later reached the Court of Appeal in Marenco v. DirecTV LLC (2015), where a putative class alleged that debit cards issued in payment of wages carried card activation fees of $.50 or $3.50 and cash withdrawal fees at ATMs, in violation of section 212; the appellate decision, however, addressed only the enforceability of an arbitration agreement and class-action waiver, and did not decide the section 212 claim.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-11]
  "The imposition of a fee in order to readily access one's earned and paid wages under a payroll card program which is designed to discharge the employer's wage payment obligations could impermissibly interfere with an employee's receipt of paid wages by creating a financial condition which would have the effect of reducing or discounting wages because such fee would be charged against the same account in which wages are deposited."
  — DLSE Opinion Letter 2008.07.07, Payroll/Debit Cards — Payment of Wages, Labor Code §§ 212 and 213 (July 7, 2008), DLSE Op. Letter 2008.07.07, at 8 (https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/opinions/2008-07-07.pdf)
  "The employee thus has access to his full wages on the scheduled pay day and thus, the payroll card programs as described to DLSE do not violate the above stated wage payment provisions."
  — DLSE Opinion Letter 2008.07.07, Payroll/Debit Cards — Payment of Wages, Labor Code §§ 212 and 213 (July 7, 2008), DLSE Op. Letter 2008.07.07, at 9 (https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/opinions/2008-07-07.pdf)
  "The effectiveness of the described wage payment programs, in practice, will of course require that employees are fully informed of the service and procedures and that it is represented as an alternative method for wage payment for which their participation is optional."
  — DLSE Opinion Letter 2008.07.07, Payroll/Debit Cards — Payment of Wages, Labor Code §§ 212 and 213 (July 7, 2008), DLSE Op. Letter 2008.07.07, at 9 (https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/opinions/2008-07-07.pdf)
  "This opinion is based exclusively on the facts and circumstances described in your request and is given based upon your representations, express or implied, that you have provided a full and fair description of all facts and circumstances that would be pertinent to our consideration of the questions presented."
  — DLSE Opinion Letter 2008.07.07, Payroll/Debit Cards — Payment of Wages, Labor Code §§ 212 and 213 (July 7, 2008), DLSE Op. Letter 2008.07.07, at 10 (https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/opinions/2008-07-07.pdf)
  "Plaintiffs who used their debit cards to withdraw cash at ATM machines were required to pay an activation fee of either $.50 or $3.50, and a cash withdrawal fee."
  — Marenco v. DirecTV LLC (Cal. Ct. App. 2015), 233 Cal.App.4th 1409 (https://www.courts.ca.gov/opinions/archive/B238421.PDF)
  "The trial court granted the motion over Marenco’s objections that DirecTV is not a signatory to the agreement, and that the agreement’s class action waiver is unconscionable under state law."
  — Marenco v. DirecTV LLC (Cal. Ct. App. 2015), 233 Cal.App.4th 1409 (https://www.courts.ca.gov/opinions/archive/B238421.PDF)
  Known gap: The DLSE opinion letter is an agency advice letter responding to two specific requests; by its own terms it is based exclusively on the facts described in those requests and does not address other factual settings. DLSE opinion letters are not regulations and do not bind courts, although courts sometimes consider them. The letter's PDF as published by the Department of Industrial Relations is a scanned image with optical-character-recognition text containing recognition errors (for example, "payrnll" for "payroll" and "mid" for "and" in its quotation of section 212); the passages quoted here were selected from portions where the recognized text is clean, and each was verified against two independent fetches of the PDF, which were byte-identical. Marenco is cited only for its description of the allegations and its procedural disposition; the Court of Appeal did not rule on whether card fees violate section 212, and the subsequent outcome of the arbitration is not reported in the opinion. The letter discusses the federal Electronic Fund Transfer Act and Regulation E at length; the current Regulation E rule is quoted from the eCFR in the following clause rather than from the letter, because the regulation has been renumbered (from 12 C.F.R. Part 205 to Part 1005) and amended since 2008.

FEDERAL OVERLAY: REGULATION E'S BAN ON REQUIRING AN ACCOUNT AT A PARTICULAR INSTITUTION
A federal rule operates alongside section 213(d)'s voluntariness condition. Regulation E, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's implementing regulation under the Electronic Fund Transfer Act, provides in 12 C.F.R. § 1005.10(e)(2) that no financial institution or other person may require a consumer to establish an account for receipt of electronic fund transfers with a particular institution as a condition of employment or receipt of a government benefit. The 2008 DLSE opinion letter described in the preceding clauses noted the same rule in its then-current form (12 C.F.R. § 205.10(e)) as further mandating the optional nature of an employee's participation in a payroll-card program, and observed that, since a 2007 amendment, payroll card accounts established through an employer for recurring deposit of wages are covered accounts under Regulation E, so that its disclosure, error-resolution, and liability-limit protections apply to them.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-11]
  "(2) Employment or government benefit. No financial institution or other person may require a consumer to establish an account for receipt of electronic fund transfers with a particular institution as a condition of employment or receipt of a government benefit."
  — 12 C.F.R. § 1005.10(e)(2) (Regulation E — Electronic Fund Transfers; eCFR current text), 12 C.F.R. § 1005.10(e)(2) (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-12/chapter-X/part-1005/subpart-A/section-1005.10)
  "Also, the optional nature of an employee's participation is further mandated under FRB's Regulation E which states: "No financial institution or other person may require a consumer to establish an account for receipt of electronic fund transfers with a particular institution as a condition of employment or receipt of governmental benefit.""
  — DLSE Opinion Letter 2008.07.07, Payroll/Debit Cards — Payment of Wages, Labor Code §§ 212 and 213 (July 7, 2008), DLSE Op. Letter 2008.07.07, at 6 (https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/opinions/2008-07-07.pdf)
  "Effective July 1, 2007, the FRB expressly made electronic "payroll cards" subject to the EFT A."

expectedJSON.body: Acme, Inc. maintains this information sheet to describe what California law says about the form in which wages may be paid to an employee such as Jordan Lee — that is, not when or how much must be paid, but what kind of instrument or method an employer may use to deliver the pay. It describes the governing statute (Labor Code section 212), which restricts payment by check or other instrument to instruments that are negotiable and payable in cash, on demand, without discount, at an established place of business in California, and which prohibits payment in scrip, coupons, or cards redeemable in merchandise; the statutory exceptions in Labor Code section 213, including voluntarily authorized direct deposit; the criminal and civil-penalty provisions attached to section 212; the published court decisions and Labor Commissioner opinion letter addressing out-of-state paychecks and payroll debit cards; and the related federal rule that an account at a particular institution may not be required as a condition of employment. It describes the law; it does not select, authorize, or change any method of payment.

Labor Code section 212(a)(1) provides that no person, or agent or officer of a person, may issue in payment of wages due, or to become due, or as an advance on wages to be earned, any order, check, draft, note, memorandum, or other acknowledgment of indebtedness unless it meets each of several conditions: it is negotiable; it is payable in cash, on demand, without discount, at some established place of business in the state; the name and address of that place of business appear on the instrument; and, at the time of issuance and for a reasonable time afterward that must be at least 30 days, the maker or drawer has sufficient funds in, or a credit, arrangement, or understanding with, the drawee for its payment. A neighboring provision, Labor Code section 208, states that all payments of wages are to be made in the manner provided by law. The Court of Appeal has described section 212 as a measure essentially intended to prevent employers from giving employees paychecks that cannot be cashed, and has summarized its accepted purpose as preventing payment of wages by orders payable only in goods or of an indefinite nature not payable on demand, or by paychecks that cannot be honored because of the drawee's insufficient funds.

This is the provision historically aimed at "company store" practices. In People v. Hampton (1965), the Court of Appeal quoted the California Supreme Court's 1916 explanation of the predecessor statute: the Legislature could be presumed to have acted because some employers had adopted the custom of paying wages by giving orders payable only in goods, or orders of an indefinite nature not payable on demand but at some future time, and the purpose of the statute was evidently to prevent the evils believed to have arisen from those practices. expectedJSON.body: Section 212(a)(1) requires that a wage instrument be payable in cash, on demand, without discount, at some established place of business in the state, and that the name and address of that place of business appear on the instrument. Section 212(c) modifies the address element when the drawee is a bank: the bank's address need not appear on the instrument, and in that case the instrument must be negotiable and payable in cash, on demand, without discount, at any place of business of the drawee chosen by the person entitled to enforce it. In Solis v. Regis Corp. (N.D. Cal. 2007), a federal district court applied these provisions to a California employer whose payroll checks were drawn on a Chicago bank. The court noted it was undisputed that under federal law banks may hold out-of-state checks for up to five days, and held that the employer violated section 212 by paying employees with checks that did not provide the name and address of a California business that would cash the checks on demand and without discount — regardless of whether a given employee was actually injured. The court also held that a fee the named plaintiff paid to cash her checks had to be construed as a "discount" within the meaning of the statute.

expectedJSON.body: Section 212(a)(1) requires that, at the time a wage instrument is issued and for a reasonable time afterward — which must be at least 30 days — the maker or drawer have sufficient funds in, or a credit, arrangement, or understanding with, the drawee for its payment. Section 212(b) supplies an evidentiary rule for enforcement: where an instrument is protested or dishonored, the notice or memorandum of protest or dishonor is admissible as proof of presentation, nonpayment, and protest, and is presumptive evidence of knowledge of insufficiency of funds or credit with the drawee. In People v. Hampton (1965), a criminal prosecution of employers whose payroll checks were dishonored, the Court of Appeal held that section 212(a) does not impose absolute criminal liability without regard to fault, but that once the prosecution establishes the facts giving rise to the statutory presumption, the burden shifts to the defendant to present evidence of justification. The court stated that an employer who pays by check is chargeable with knowledge of all that the employer reasonably should have known as well as what the employer actually knew, and must show that nonpayment of the checks resulted from circumstances neither foreseeable nor preventable by reasonably prudent investigation or action.

expectedJSON.body: Two enforcement provisions attach to section 212. Labor Code section 215 makes any person, or the agent, manager, superintendent, or officer of a person, who violates section 212 (among other listed sections) guilty of a misdemeanor. Labor Code section 225.5 provides that, in addition to and independent of any other penalty in the article, every person who unlawfully withholds wages due any employee in violation of section 212, 216, 221, 222, or 223 is subject to a civil penalty of $100 for each failure to pay each employee for an initial violation, and $200 for each failure to pay each employee plus 25 percent of the amount unlawfully withheld for each subsequent, willful, or intentional violation; the penalty is recovered by the Labor Commissioner in a wage hearing or an independent civil action brought in the name of the people of the State of California. In Solis v. Regis Corp., the federal district court read the section 225.5 penalty as limited to section 212 violations that actually involve a withholding of wages — such as a check-cashing fee or a bank hold — and held that where an employee cashed the check on demand without a fee there was no withholding even if the check was drawn on an out-of-state bank; for section 212 violations not involving a withholding, the court concluded the default civil penalty of the Private Attorneys General Act (Labor Code section 2699(f)) applied instead.

(b) For each subsequent violation, or any willful or intentional violation, two hundred dollars ($200) for each failure to pay each employee, plus 25 percent of the amount unlawfully withheld. The penalty shall be recovered by the Labor Commissioner as part of a hearing held to recover unpaid wages and penalties or in an independent civil action.

Under subdivision (d), nothing in section 212 prohibits an employer from depositing wages due or to become due, or an advance on wages to be earned, in an account in any bank, savings and loan association, or credit union of the employee's choice with a place of business located in this state, provided that the employee has voluntarily authorized that deposit. expectedJSON.body: No California statute specifically addresses payroll debit cards, and no published California appellate decision located for this document decides whether a particular payroll-card program complies with sections 212 and 213. The most detailed public authority is a July 7, 2008 opinion letter of the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement analyzing two national payroll-card programs. The letter treated the programs first as direct deposit under section 213(d) — concluding that the voluntariness condition was satisfied because employee participation was optional and employees retained the option of direct deposit to an institution of their own choosing — and then applied the section 212(a) requirement that wages be payable in cash without discount to the card itself. The letter stated that imposing a fee to access one's earned wages under such a program could impermissibly interfere with receipt of paid wages by reducing or discounting them, but concluded that programs providing at least one fee-free transaction per pay period, giving the employee access to full wages in cash on the scheduled payday, did not violate the wage payment provisions as described, and that their effectiveness in practice would require that employees be fully informed and that the card be presented as an optional alternative. The letter also stated that the itemized wage statement requirement of Labor Code section 226(a) continues to apply. The fact pattern the letter warned about later reached the Court of Appeal in Marenco v. DirecTV LLC (2015), where a putative class alleged that debit cards issued in payment of wages carried card activation fees of $.50 or $3.50 and cash withdrawal fees at ATMs, in violation of section 212; the appellate decision, however, addressed only the enforceability of an arbitration agreement and class-action waiver, and did not decide the section 212 claim.

Nothing in section 212 prohibits an employer from guaranteeing payment of bills incurred by an employee for the necessaries of life or for tools and implements used in the employee's duties (subdivision (a)); section 212 does not apply to counties, municipal corporations, quasi-municipal corporations, or school districts (subdivision (b)); and it does not apply to students of nonprofit schools, colleges, universities, and other nonprofit educational institutions (subdivision (c)). Labor Code section 220(b) separately provides that sections 200 through 211 and sections 215 through 219 do not apply to the payment of wages of employees directly employed by any county, incorporated city, or town or other municipal corporation, while all other employments are subject to those provisions. Section 220(a), which lists the wage-payment sections that do not apply to employees directly employed by the State of California, does not list section 212; consistent with that, the Brown decision described above reached the merits of a section 212 claim brought on behalf of state correctional employees, rejecting it on the ground that accrued furlough credits were not a "payment" governed by the statute.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 213(a)–(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Nothing contained in Section 212 shall: (a) Prohibit an employer from guaranteeing the payment of bills incurred by an employee for the necessaries of life or for the tools and implements used by the employee in the performance of his or her duties. (b) Apply to counties, municipal corporations, quasi-municipal corporations, or school districts. (c) Apply to students of nonprofit schools, colleges, universities, and other nonprofit educational institutions.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 220(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Sections 200 to 211, inclusive, and Sections 215 to 219, inclusive, do not apply to the payment of wages of employees directly employed by any county, incorporated city, or town or other municipal corporation. All other employments are subject to these provisions.

citations.case: Brown v. Superior Court (Cal. Ct. App. 2011)
citations.quote: We thus agree with the Governor that section 212 has no applicability here, and does not create a ministerial duty warranting the issuance of a writ of mandate.

Section 220(a) is described but not quoted; it lists sections 201.3, 201.5, 201.6, 201.7, 201.8, 203.1, 203.5, 204, 204a, 204b, 204c, 204.1, 205, and 205.5 as inapplicable to state employees, and section 212 is not among them. Section 212 is within the 200–211 range excluded for county and municipal employees by section 220(b), so that exclusion overlaps section 213(b); the two provisions use different lists of entities (section 213(b) names school districts and quasi-municipal corporations; section 220(b) names counties, incorporated cities, towns, and other municipal corporations), and no source fetched for this document reconciles them. The characterization of Brown's holding is drawn from the opinion's discussion described in the first clause; Brown quoted the trial court's finding that a furlough credit "does not constitute ‘payment’ for any work day" and agreed section 212 had no applicability.
